# Ultraviolet follow-up of OGLE-SMC-ECL-06090

## Swift detects both eclipses in UVW1

Swift UVOT records two ultraviolet dips at phases predicted by earlier OGLE optical photometry. From 275 exposures on 267 UT nights, their fitted fractional depths were 0.412 ± 0.031 and 0.318 ± 0.054 (night-cluster standard errors). These are differential aperture-flux deficits relative to the median off-eclipse flux ratio. Nearby blended flux, coincidence losses, small-aperture corrections and instrumental throughput can affect the depths. All three apertures recovered both eclipses. A comparison star 29.7″ away gave −0.008 ± 0.035 and −0.016 ± 0.025 at the target's phases. None of the 79 tested phase displacements fit the target series better. Some displacements trade the primary and secondary, and the trials are correlated; these are template checks.

The first accepted exposure began at 01:20:18 UTC on 2012 September 25 and the last ended at 14:54:51 UTC on 2026 October 7. The 2012 data come from one long visit split into nine snapshots, including one near secondary eclipse. This single-night sequence contains pre-eclipse baseline, two dim snapshots spanning the expected center and recovery. At fixed OGLE Gaussian width, an exposure-integrated profile fit to Swift gave secondary phase 0.49535 (conditional profile 95% interval 0.4892–0.5091), 2.5 minutes before the OGLE prediction of 0.49682. Changing the width from 0.018 to 0.035 cycles changes the phase estimate from 0.4909 to 0.50495. It supplies no primary time on that night. In 2025, 25 accepted measurements sampled one primary and one secondary half-depth core. All three 2026 exposures fell outside both half-depth cores. These data do not locate a new 2026 time of minimum.

### How much of the timing motion can Swift detect?

The two broad time groups below were chosen retrospectively to split the relatively regular 2016–2026 observing sequence. They omit the isolated 2012 visit. The orbital period was fixed to the optical catalog value. Each group had a free primary and secondary center and a free depth for each dip. The widths were taken from the OGLE flux fit. Each calendar year had its own baseline.

| Observation years | Exposures | Independently fitted interval | Night-cluster standard error |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2016–2020 | 124 | 14.656 h | 0.144 h |
| 2021–2026 | 142 | 15.495 h | 0.373 h |

The difference is +50.3 min. A 999-replicate observing-night bootstrap, stratified by calendar year, gave a percentile interval of +1.6 to +115.9 min. Aperture radii of 2.7″ and 4.5″ gave +49.8 and +41.2 min. Fitting the widths gave +49.0 min in the 3.5″ aperture. The late secondary is shallow and sparse, so its fitted centroid and depth trade against each other. The results are conditional on selection, noise prescription and eclipse template.

A separate fit held the OGLE-predicted differential timing trajectory fixed in shape and varied its amplitude. Two phase zero points and a common linear ephemeris drift were free. Swift recovered 0.92 ± 0.41 times the optical trajectory, with error clustered by night. The weighted sum of squared residuals was 273.66 for zero motion and 270.57 for the nominal optical motion under this fit. Absolute predictions from the OGLE-only cubic and first-order precession models scored 271.54 and 272.10; their predictions are indistinguishable here. In the separate all-epochs fit, moving each predicted eclipse center by its own fitted offset produced a relative separation correction of +5.7 ± 9.4 min. This latter fit pools all years against the *changing* OGLE prediction.

### Images and photometry

The HEASARC swiftmastr cone query covered all pointings within 0.20° of the target. Of 295 listed pointings, 287 had positive UVW1 catalog exposure and their calibrated sky images were retrieved from the public archive. Swift UVOT field size and resolution make the test sensitive to crowding and partial exposures. The extraction keeps 97 × 97 count-image stamps only when fully on the image array, and uses matching exposure-map stamps. Local exposure as well as actual positive counts were required. The archive product URLs and byte digests are in swift-receipts.json. Archive scope is conditional on this cone and filter.

Align each aperture to the bright Gaia source 4686449235706531584, 19.1″ away, by measuring its centroid in that image. Reject corrections exceeding 3.4″ and background/exposure-map discontinuities. Sum counts within the circular aperture; estimate the background in a 6.5–10.5″ annulus and scale by the summed exposure map. Apply the same aperture to the bright reference and a check source, Gaia 4686449029548388352. Divide target by reference rate, use the propagated counting error plus a 6% fractional floor, and restrict both local exposures to >20 s. Changing the aperture size, forgoing differential calibration, fitting the widths, and moving the trial phases are included outputs. The method is for *relative* time-domain photometry; it does not convert count rates to calibrated source luminosities. Geocentric heliocentric corrections neglect the low-Earth-orbit spacecraft term, below 0.03 seconds for Swift. The XMM orbital correction can be up to approximately half a second. Source TT-to-UTC timestamp conventions and timing calibration are immaterial at the tens-of-minutes scale used here.

## Independent XMM-Newton UVM2 primary eclipse

Observation 0741450101 on 2015 March 24–25 supplies twelve archival Optical Monitor source lists. The target is matched at 0.6–1.0″ in the individual exposures. In three UVM2 integrations the Vega magnitudes were 16.442 ± 0.037, 16.866 ± 0.050 and 16.435 ± 0.037. The middle exposure was **0.428 ± 0.056 mag** fainter than the average of the flanking two. The pipeline quality flag was zero throughout. Among 75 matched field controls with similar brightness and the same quality criteria, the median differential change was +0.0004 mag and robust scatter 0.048 mag. None was fainter by as much as the target. The midpoint at 19:35:47 UTC was 28 minutes after the OGLE-predicted primary center, inside its 66.7-minute integration. This observes eclipse dimming directly; the exposure cannot determine its central time by itself. UV color measurements made in separate filters at different orbital phases should not be interpreted as a simultaneous stellar spectrum.

## Gaia color photometry

Accepted Gaia DR3 epoch data provided 45 BP and 43 RP transit fluxes. Conditional on the OGLE phase and widths, fitted primary and secondary fractional depths in BP were 0.416 ± 0.044 and 0.386 ± 0.024; in RP, 0.230 ± 0.055 and 0.425 ± 0.138. Errors are clustered by observing night. Each band has only three primary and two secondary half-depth-core points. BP and RP share Gaia visits with the previous G-band check. Color, source blending and instrumental calibration prevent inferring component temperatures from these fits. Gaia's primary archive marks no public XP continuous/sampled spectrum, RVS spectrum or epoch radial velocities for this source.

## Replay and credits

Run the Python scripts from this directory with NumPy, SciPy, Astropy and PyERFA. The checked-in differential Swift photometry replays with `python swift_fit.py`, `python swift_motion.py` and `python swift_2012.py`. Use `python gaia_colors.py` for Gaia. The public table queries are in inputs/sources.json. For an XMM pixel-catalog replay, run `python fetch_xmm.py` followed by `python xmm.py`. For Swift image-level reproduction run `python swift_stamps.py`, `python swift_exposure.py`, `python swift_photometry.py`, then the fit commands. The frozen inventory for that retrieval is included. Verify the retrieved image and exposure hashes against swift-receipts.json. Running coverage.py after image retrieval writes swift-receipts-replayed.json for comparison with the original receipts.

Observations and calibration credit the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, the S-CUBED survey and other pointed-observation investigators, the NASA HEASARC, the ESA XMM-Newton Science Operations Centre and Survey Science Centre, the Gaia and DPAC collaborations, and the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment. The accompanying OGLE fit parameters were obtained from 1,348 public OGLE-III/IV I-band observations.
